questions.question: Why is cache invalidation considered one of the hardest problems in computer science?

options.text: It requires specialized hardware that most organizations cannot afford
Knowing when data changed and ensuring all distributed caches are updated consistently involves complex coordination
Cache invalidation algorithms are protected by patents from major tech companies
Modern cloud platforms have eliminated this problem entirely

questions.explanation: In distributed systems, data changes in one place but may be cached in many locations. Ensuring all caches are invalidated consistently, handling race conditions, network partitions, and avoiding stale data while maintaining performance is genuinely difficult. Facebook processes millions of cache invalidations per second across thousands of servers. The famous quote from Phil Karlton: 'There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.' This is not hyperbole.

questions.question: What are the main cache invalidation strategies? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Time-based invalidation using TTL expiration
Event-based invalidation triggered by data changes
Version-based invalidation using cache key versioning
Probabilistic invalidation using random sampling

questions.explanation: TTL: entries expire after a set time, simple but allows bounded staleness. Event-based: invalidate immediately when source changes, provides freshness but requires infrastructure. Version-based: include version in cache key, new version means new key, old entries expire naturally. Each has tradeoffs. Netflix uses TTL for most content metadata, event-based for user preferences, and version-based for A/B test configurations. Probabilistic invalidation would cause unpredictable, inconsistent behavior.

questions.question: A user updates their profile, but the old profile still shows on the website. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The database transaction failed to commit the update
The cache was not invalidated after the database update
The user's browser has corrupted local storage
The application server crashed during the request

questions.explanation: This is the classic cache invalidation failure: database updated successfully but cache still holds old data. The application should invalidate or update the cache entry when the profile changes. This bug is so common it has a name: 'stale cache.' Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram have all had public incidents caused by cache invalidation bugs. The fix: ensure every write path includes cache invalidation, and test invalidation as rigorously as you test the write itself.

questions.question: What is 'write-through' caching?

options.text: Periodically deleting cache entries based on access patterns
Writing to both cache and database simultaneously, keeping them in sync
Writing only to cache and ignoring the database
Bypassing cache entirely for all write operations

questions.explanation: Write-through updates both cache and database on every write operation. The cache is always current, eliminating the need for invalidation. The tradeoff: writes are slower because they must complete in both systems. This pattern is good for read-heavy workloads where consistency is critical and write volume is manageable. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) uses write-through. The alternative, write-behind, writes to cache first and asynchronously updates the database, which is faster but risks data loss.

questions.question: What is the 'cache-aside' invalidation pattern?

options.text: The cache automatically detects and invalidates stale entries
The application explicitly deletes the cache entry when data changes
Cache entries are never invalidated, only replaced
The database triggers cache invalidation through stored procedures

questions.explanation: In cache-aside, the application manages invalidation explicitly: on update, delete the cache entry. The next read will miss cache, fetch from database, and repopulate cache. This is simple and gives full control but requires discipline. Every code path that modifies data must remember to invalidate cache. A common bug: adding a new update endpoint and forgetting cache invalidation. Code reviews should specifically check for this. Some teams use aspect-oriented programming to automate invalidation.

questions.question: A distributed system has caches in multiple regions. How can cache invalidation be coordinated across regions?

options.text: Cross-region cache invalidation is impossible to implement reliably
Publish invalidation events to a message queue that all regions subscribe to
Use a single global cache to avoid coordination complexity
Disable caching entirely in multi-region deployments

questions.explanation: Pub/sub systems like Kafka or Redis Pub/Sub can broadcast invalidation events. When data changes, publish an invalidation event; all regions receive it and invalidate their local caches. Eventual consistency applies because there is propagation delay. Facebook's cache invalidation system uses this pattern, processing millions of invalidations per second. The tradeoff: added infrastructure complexity and eventual consistency. For strong consistency, you would need synchronous invalidation, which adds latency.

questions.question: What is a potential race condition in cache invalidation?

options.text: Cache operations executing faster than expected
Stale data being written to cache after invalidation due to concurrent operations
Cache keys exceeding maximum length limits
Too many cache hits overwhelming the cache server

questions.explanation: Classic race condition: Thread A reads old data from database, Thread B updates database and invalidates cache, Thread A writes old data to cache. Now cache has stale data despite invalidation. Solutions include: versioning (include version in cache key), distributed locks (serialize access), or delete-after-write patterns (delete cache after write completes, not before). This race condition has caused outages at major companies. It is subtle and easy to miss in code review.

questions.question: Does TTL-based invalidation guarantee that cached data is never stale?

options.text: Yes, TTL ensures data is always fresh within the specified time window
No, data can be stale from the moment it is cached until TTL expires
Yes, if TTL is set to a sufficiently short duration
No, but only during network partitions

questions.explanation: TTL only guarantees data will not be stale for longer than the TTL duration. Data can be stale from the moment it is cached until TTL expires. If you cache data with a 5-minute TTL and the source changes 1 second later, the cache serves stale data for 4 minutes and 59 seconds. For strong consistency, event-based invalidation is needed. TTL provides bounded staleness, which is acceptable for many use cases but not all. Choose TTL based on acceptable staleness, not arbitrary round numbers.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'purge' and 'ban' in cache invalidation systems like Varnish?

options.text: They are synonymous terms for the same operation
Purge removes specific URLs immediately; Ban marks patterns as invalid without immediate removal
Purge is faster but less reliable than ban
Ban is a deprecated feature replaced by purge

questions.explanation: Purge immediately removes a specific cached object from memory. Ban adds a rule that marks matching objects as invalid on access (lazy invalidation). Ban is useful for pattern-based invalidation (invalidate all product pages) without scanning the entire cache. Varnish checks ban rules on each request; if an object matches a ban rule newer than the object, it is considered invalid. Bans accumulate and are periodically cleaned up. Use purge for specific URLs, ban for patterns.

questions.question: How does cache key versioning help with invalidation?

options.text: It does not help with invalidation, only with debugging
New version means new cache key, so old entries are naturally ignored and expire
It makes cache lookups faster through version indexing
It encrypts cache entries for security

questions.explanation: Include version in cache key: user:123:v2. When data changes, increment version to v3. Old entries (v1, v2) are never accessed again and expire naturally via TTL or eviction. No explicit invalidation needed. The tradeoff: uses more memory temporarily (old and new versions coexist) and requires tracking current version somewhere. This pattern is elegant for scenarios where you can easily track versions, like database row versions or deployment versions.

questions.question: A CDN caches a page with incorrect data. What is the fastest way to fix this?

options.text: Wait for the TTL to expire naturally
Send a purge or invalidation request to the CDN API
Restart all CDN edge servers
Change the page URL to bypass the cached version

questions.explanation: CDNs provide purge or invalidation APIs to remove specific URLs or patterns from edge caches. This is faster than waiting for TTL. CloudFront, Fastly, and Cloudflare all support invalidation APIs. Some CDNs also support cache tags for grouped invalidation (invalidate all pages tagged 'product-123'). Changing the URL (cache busting) works but is disruptive to users and SEO. Restarting edge servers is not possible for most CDN customers and would cause massive disruption.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'soft' and 'hard' cache invalidation?

options.text: Soft invalidation uses less memory than hard invalidation
Soft marks as stale but serves while refreshing; Hard removes immediately forcing a wait
Hard invalidation is more secure than soft invalidation
These terms refer to hardware-based versus software-based caching

questions.explanation: Soft invalidation (stale-while-revalidate): serve stale data immediately while fetching fresh data in background. The user gets fast response with potentially stale data. Hard invalidation: remove immediately, next request waits for fresh data. The user gets fresh data but waits longer. HTTP Cache-Control supports stale-while-revalidate directive. Soft invalidation improves availability and perceived performance at the cost of temporary staleness. Choose based on freshness requirements.
